LESSON 58 OF 106·Data Protection and Endpoint Security

Backups: The 3-2-1 Rule and Tested Restores

Why three copies on two media with one offsite survives ransomware that a synchronised drive does not — and why an untested backup is only a hypothesis about recovery.

Beginner13 min
Why this matters

A backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis, not a control. The rule of three copies is well known; the part everyone gets wrong is the test.

  1. Verification: Follow three copies, two media, one off site, and make the off-site copy immutable.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Three copies means the original plus two backups, so one failure is survivable.
  • Two media means the copies are not all on the same device that can fail together.
  • One off site means a fire, theft or ransomware at the primary location does not destroy everything.
  • Incremental and full backups trade speed against restore time, since a restore of many incrementals is slower.
  • Retention determines what point you can return to, so a ransomware event may exceed the shortest retention.

The background

  • Backups were tape-based, offsite by definition, and slow enough that testing was routine.
  • Cheap disk arrays made local backups affordable and, with them, the assumption that the copy was safe.
  • Synchronised storage made replication continuous, which quietly turned a backup into a mirror of the primary.
  • Ransomware made immutability the main requirement, because anything writable by the attacker is not a backup.

Real-world examples

  • A synchronised folder is not a backup, since deletion or encryption propagates to the copy immediately.
  • A restore that has never been timed turns a four-hour outage into a four-day outage.
  • Backups with a retention shorter than the attacker dwell time can be entirely deleted before anyone notices.

What to look for

  • Check whether the backup copy is genuinely separate, or synchronised to the primary.
  • Check whether backups are protected from deletion by the same credentials that run production.
  • Check the last time a full restore was actually performed and timed.
  • Check the retention period against the time an attacker could plausibly remain undetected.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Follow three copies, two media, one off site, and make the off-site copy immutable.
  • Use separate credentials for backup administration and require multi-factor authentication on it.
  • Test restores regularly and record the real elapsed time for a full recovery.
  • Alert on backup deletion, since that is a strong indicator of an ongoing incident.
  • Include configuration and identity data in backups, since restoring only data often leaves a system unusable.
